blocks.text: It is proved that חומט chomet is a lizard living in the sand, which the Arabs call حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca.

For the more recent Hebrews, Solomon, Kimchi, Pomarius and Aquinas, חומט chomet is the limax [slug]. Nor do those Spaniards mean anything else who in Kimchi render it in the vernacular as כרבר. For one should read כר״כול caracol, which is what they call the slug. This is followed by Arias, Münster, Pierre Robert, the Genevans and the English, who here too have limax [slug]. The ancients, however, thought otherwise. For to the Greeks and to Jerome חומט chomet is σαῦρα [saura], a lizard. And in the printed Arabic versions it is حربا [ḥirbā] chirba, the chameleon; in the manuscript ones سام ابرص [sām abraṣ] sammabras, the stellio. Nor does the Syriac ܚܘܠܡܛܐ chaulmata mean anything else here, according to Gabriel Sionita, whom I prefer to believe rather than Battista Ferrari, who renders it: a bird having a back marked with black and purple feathers; plainly ἀπροσδιονύσως [aprosdionysōs]. For the subject here is not birds but creeping things of the earth. Therefore, like the preceding ones, חומט chomet also seems to belong to the lizard kind. Nor is the origin of the word obscure. For to the Talmudists חומטון chometon is sand. Hence in the tractate On the Sabbath, ch. 5, fol. 54a (where the Talmudists discuss why in 1 Reg. IX, 13 Hiram, king of the Tyrians, called ארץ כבול, the land of Chabul, the district which Solomon had given him), R. Nachman, son of Isaac, says: [col. 1076] ארץ חומטין היתה אמאי קרו לה כבול דמשתרגה בה כרעא עד כבלא It was a land of chometon; hence they called it the land of chabul, because in it the leg sank down to the ankle. And Kimchi, citing this passage in his Lexicon under the root כבל, though with slightly altered words, explains חומטון chometon as חול chol, that is, sand. So for them land of chometon is land of sand, or sandy land. Baal Aruch likewise explains the whole passage thus: פי׳ שרגליו של אדם משתקעות בה מחמת החול כאילו הן כבולין לכן אינה עושה פירות It means that a man's feet sank into it (the land) because of the (abundance of) sand, as if they had been [II, 501] fettered, and that it was therefore unfruitful. In the Gloss on the Talmud, the land of chometon is land מלחה ומתבקעת, salty and cracked. And in ch. 2 of the same tractate, fol. 31a, חומטון for the Glossator is ארץ מלחה ומשמרת את הפירות מהתליע, salty soil, which preserves fruits from worms. But the former interpretation is the truer, and suits both passages exceedingly well. For sand is both troublesome to the feet of those walking, and in hot places has a ἀρτυτικὴν [artytikēn] power, by which it preserves things from corruption for a long time. Thus many assert that in the sands of Africa corpses are embalmed and sold as mummy. Indeed the word חומטון chometon, although it does not occur in the Prophetic books, seems to be very ancient ^{(1)}. And I think the Greeks, dropping the aspiration, derived from it ἄμαθον [amathon], and, with a prefix, ψάμαθον [psamathon]. Both are found in the most ancient writers, Homer for instance and others, in the sense of sand. Yet the Grammarians hold that ἄμαθον [amathon] is μεσόγειον [mesogeion], inland sand, and ψάμαθον [psamathon] παραθαλασσίαν [parathalassian], or shore sand. So, roughly, Hesychius, the Suda and others distinguish them.

Therefore, just as חימטון chometon is sand, so חומט chomet is a species of lizard that lives in the sands. And it seems that the Arabs' حلكا [ḥlkā] chulaca, or لحكا [lḥkā] lucha, and luchaca, is meant; of which Alcamus says: الحلكا دويبة تغوص في الرمل او ضرب من العظا كالحلكا [al-ḥlkā duwaybba taghūṣu fī al-raml aw ḍarb min al-ʿaẓā ka-al-ḥlkā] Alchulaca, a little animal that plunges into the sand; or a species of lizard, which is also called chulaca. The same: اللحكا دويبة زرقا تشبه العظا [al-lḥkā duwaybba zarqā tushbihu al-ʿaẓā] Luchaca, a little blue animal, like a lizard. Damir: لحلكا دويبة شبيهة بالعغناة تغوص في الرمل [lḥlkā duwaybba shabīha bi-al-ʿghnāt taghūṣu fī al-raml] Alchulaca, a little animal like a lizard, which plunges into the sands. Alazhari: اللحكا دويبة كانها سمكة تكون في الرمل فاذا احست الانسان دارت في الرمل وغاصت فيه [al-lḥkā duwaybba ka-annahā samaka takūnu fī al-raml fa-idhā aḥassat al-insān dārat fī al-raml wa-ghāṣat fīhi] Luchaca, a little animal living in the sand like a fish (in water); which, when it senses a man, rolls about in the sand and plunges into it. And Ibnosacith: اللحكا دوبة شبيهة بالعظاية وقوايم خفيفة [al-lḥkā dwba shabīha bi-al-ʿaẓāya wa-qawāyim khafīfa] Luchaca, a little animal like a lizard, with very light feet. Asseidalanius and Arruvianus: دويبة مثل الاصبع تجري في الرمل ثم تغوص [duwaybba mithl al-iṣbaʿ tajrī fī al-raml thumma taghūṣu] [col. 1077] فيه وهذا يقوي قول الجوهري انه مقلوبة من الحلكا [fīhi wa-hādhā yuqawwī qawl al-Jawharī annahu maqlūba min al-ḥlkā] [II, 502] It is a little animal the size of a finger, which runs through the sands and plunges into them. This confirms the statement of Giauhari that the name luchaca is inverted from chulaca. Again Damir: العرب تسيها بنات النقا لانها تسكن نقيات [al-ʿarab tsyhā banāt al-naqā li-annahā taskunu nqyāt] The Arabs also call them daughters of the sand-hill, because it lives in sand-hills.
